subtype: Approach: copying a funded startup's spending pattern [Pitfall]
passage: Hansa signed for a desk at the glass-walled co-working space in Bengaluru the same week she read that a rival startup had one. She hired a part-time designer, and put money into paid ads, because that was what the rival did. Kamal, the founder at the next desk, noticed her ad dashboard flickering. "Do you know how much they raised?" he asked. "About ten times what you have." Hansa shrugged. But in the second month she was checking her bank balance in the corridor by the coffee machine, where nobody could see her face. She could afford the designer for only another week. The rival kept going, because their cash could absorb it. Hansa's could not.

qa.q: Which three things did Hansa copy from the rival?
qa.a: A desk at the co-working space, a part-time designer and paid ads.

qa.q: What was Hansa feeling in the second month, and how can you tell?
qa.a: Hansa was anxious, shown by checking her balance in the corridor where nobody could see her face.

qa.q: What could Hansa do instead of copying the rival?
qa.a: Hansa could spend only on what brings the first customers and match her spending to her own cash.

qa.q: How might Kamal have felt watching Hansa's spending?
qa.a: Kamal was probably concerned, as the question about how much the rival raised suggests.

grounding: Hansa copies a funded rival's desk, designer and paid ads, but the rival's much larger cash means the same pattern burns her out.

subtype: Approach: copying a funded startup's spending pattern [Pitfall]
passage:
Dear Neelam,
In January you asked why I was renting a desk in that glass co-working building when I could work from home. I said, "Because that's what serious startups do." I owe you a more honest answer.
I was copying the meal-kit startup across town. They had a smart desk, a full-time designer and ads everywhere. So I got the desk, hired a designer and started ads too. What I didn't think about is that they had raised roughly ten times what I had saved.
By May my money was nearly gone. I had forty customers and a beautiful brand. I had also stopped sleeping properly and snapped at my designer, who didn't deserve it.
I've given up the desk and paused the ads. I'd like to come and talk about what a plan my size looks like. Is next week possible?
Pema

qa.q: Why did Pema say the co-working desk was needed?
How does Pema feel looking back at copying the rival?
qa.a: Pema feels regretful and worn out, having burned through savings and snapped at the designer.

qa.q: What would you change first in Pema's approach?
qa.a: Plan spending from Pema's own savings, starting small, such as working from home and testing sales before paying for ads.

qa.q: How might the designer have experienced those months?
qa.a: The designer was snapped at without deserving it and may have felt hurt and unsure about the job.

grounding: It shows a first-time founder copying a funded rival's desk, designer and ads without its money, so the same spending burns through savings.

subtype: Approach: copying a funded startup's spending pattern [Pitfall]
passage:
Devika, you want the embarrassing version? Fine. I'm Ganga. Two years ago I started a tutoring platform, and every morning I scrolled through what the big funded one in Bengaluru was doing. They had a designer, so I hired a designer. They had a desk in a fancy co-working space, so I got one too. They ran ads on every video site, so I ran ads. I felt like a real founder for about four months.
What I never asked was how much money they had. Later I read it in a business article: roughly ten times my whole savings. Same spending, a tenth of the fuel. By month six I was working nights to pay the designer and crying in the co-working washroom.
If I did it again, Devika, I'd copy their curiosity, not their costs.

qa.q: What did Ganga later learn about the rival's money?
qa.a: They had roughly ten times Ganga's whole savings.

qa.q: What was Ganga feeling during the first four months?
qa.a: Ganga felt proud, like a real founder, before the money pressure turned it into exhaustion and distress.

qa.q: What does "copy their curiosity, not their costs" suggest Ganga would do next time?
qa.a: Learn from how rivals test ideas, but plan spending around Ganga's own savings rather than their budget.

qa.q: How might the designer be affected when the money ran low?
qa.a: The designer's pay depended on Ganga working nights, so the job was far less secure than it looked.

grounding: It shows a founder copying a well-funded rival's designer, desk and ads with a tenth of the money, which drains the savings and exhausts the founder.
